blocks.markdown: SSS contributions, remittance, records, and penalties — objectives: apply the current contribution schedule (Sec. 4(a)(9) + 2025 circulars), state each payer's duties (Secs. 18–21), run the remittance and records machinery (Secs. 22–24-A), invoke the exemptions (Secs. 16–17), and map criminal and civil liability (Sec. 28) through Ambassador Hotel.

This lesson follows syllabus items II.3–II.7 in order: exemptions (Secs. 16–17), contributions (Secs. 4(a)(9), 8(i), 18–21), remittance (Secs. 22–23), employment records and reports (Secs. 24, 24-A), and penalties (Sec. 28). Read it as the money pipeline: who pays, when, how it is collected, what records prove it, and what happens when it fails.

Sec. 16 builds a triple shield: the SSS itself (assets, contributions, accruals, earnings, papers) is exempt from all taxes, assessments, fees, charges, and import duties — pierceable only by a tax measure **expressly revoking** the Sec. 2 policy; benefit payments are exempt from all taxes, fees, and charges; and benefits are immune from **attachment, garnishment, levy, or seizure**, before or after receipt. The **sole exception**: collecting the member's own debt to the SSS. Creditors cannot garnish pensions; payroll must not withhold tax on benefit advances.

Sec. 17's rule is **zero fees** for handling SSS benefit claims — any charge agreement or benefit deduction for that purpose is void. The single exception needs all four conditions: a **Philippine Bar member**, appearing as counsel in a **Commission case**, capped at **10%** of benefits awarded, payable **only after actual payment**. Violation draws P500–P5,000 and/or 6 months to 1 year. Fixers taking a cut of a member's benefit are acting unlawfully on the face of the statute.

Sec. 4(a)(9) ramps the rate from 12% (2019) to the **current 15% — employer 10%, employee 5% — on MSC P5,000–P35,000**, implemented by SSS Circulars No. 2024-006 (employers/employees), 2024-007 (household/kasambahay), 2024-008 (self-employed), 2024-009 (voluntary/non-working spouse), and 2024-010 (land-based OFW), all effective **1 January 2025** and still the latest tables on sss.gov.ph as of 9 November 2026. MSC above P20,000 goes to the MPF (MySSS Pension Booster); EC stays employer-only at P10/P30; land-based OFW minimum MSC is P8,000; kasambahays below the minimum pay on actual salary while other off-band members pay on the band edges.

Secs. 18–19 split the monthly duty: the employer **deducts and withholds** the employee share (today 5% of MSC) and **pays its own share** (today 10%) — and is absolutely barred from shifting its share to employees, **notwithstanding any contract to the contrary**, not even with written employee consent. Remittances ride on a **quarterly collection list** (employer ID, employee names and SSS numbers, quarterly totals) — the paper trail examiners reconcile against payroll registers.

Sec. 19-A: self-employed members pay **both shares on declared earnings** (today 15% of the matching MSC, Circular 2024-008), the registration declaration fixing the MSC until superseded by a later declaration. Micro-earners at P1,000/month or below may get reductions; members 55 and above face once-a-year increase limits. The declaration is doing double duty — contribution base today, AMSC benefit base tomorrow — so realistic declarations matter.

Secs. 20–21 close the funding picture: Congress annually appropriates the SSS's **operating expenses plus actuarial top-ups** to keep an adequate working balance (Sec. 20), and the Republic **guarantees solvency and non-diminution of benefits** (Sec. 21). Benefits may expand on actuarial soundness but can never be cut by fiat. The complete 'who contributes' answer: employee + employer + self-employed/voluntary (both shares) + government (operations and adequacy).

Sec. 22 sets the pipeline deadline: remit within the **first 10 days** of the following month, with a **2%-per-month** delinquency penalty (RA 11199 rate — the 3% in older cases is pre-2019 law). Non-remittance **never prejudices the employee's benefits** — SSS pays the worker and chases the employer through tax-like collection (preferred court action or sheriff's levy warrant), within **20 years**, aided by the Sec. 22(d) presumption (last complete record or 3-year average = monthly dues until overcome). Payroll calendars must treat the 10th as a hard deadline.

Secs. 22-A–23 complete collection: self-employed members remit **quarterly** with **no retroactive payment** (the backstop of Sec. 11-A's no-backfill rule), while Sec. 23 demands complete, properly identified collection through any Commission-adopted payment mode — today's electronic collection lists and reference numbers are the descendants of its 'stamps, coupons, tickets.' Misidentified payments (wrong SSS number or employer ID) are the modern collection failure to control for.

Sec. 24 is the compliance engine. **Report every covered employee immediately** (par. a) — an unreported worker's death, sickness, disability, or 60th birthday converts into employer damages equal to the lost benefits (pensions: accumulated or **5 years' pension, higher**, plus dependents' pension), with grace only for contingencies **within 30 days of hiring**; principals are **subsidiarily liable** with contractors and must require a **surety bond**. **Misdating or under-remitting** (par. b) draws shortfall damages PLUS contributions and penalties. Records are **confidential, presumed correct**, and the adjudication basis — correct them before the benefit right accrues. Keep true work records plus the **Annual Register** filed every **January**, open to SSS inspection; require the lifetime **SSS number** at hiring (never an excuse for non-reporting); certified/archival copies equal originals; and **LGU permits require SSS clearance**, issuable within **5 working days**.

Sec. 24-A gives self-employed members **30 days from starting practice or operations** to register and report (identity, occupation, average monthly net income, dependents). The declared income becomes the Sec. 19-A contribution and benefit base — calendar it with BIR and LGU registrations. Note the contrast with Sec. 24(a): here the 30 days is a direct duty, not a damage grace period.

Sec. 28 layers liability in three bands. **Compliance offenses** (e): general failure is fine OR imprisonment OR both (P5,000–P20,000; 6y1d–12y) — but failure to **register, deduct, or remit** is fine AND imprisonment. **Fraud cluster**: false claim/loan statements (Art. 172 RPC); unentitled receipt with intent to defraud, fine AND 6y1d–12y; device dealing/forgery, OR penalties. **Accountability**: juridical entities act through humans — **managing head, directors, or partners** personally liable (f); SSS employee misappropriation → Art. 217 malversation (g); deduct-but-not-remit within **30 days** → **presumed estafa** under Art. 315 (h); and the SSS or employee may file criminally with SSS-friendly venue (i). Deduction without remittance is never a cash-flow decision — after 30 days it is presumed estafa.

blocks.markdown: Run the monthly compliance cycle. **Hiring**: collect the lifetime SSS number, classify (control test), report immediately. **Payroll**: withhold 5%, accrue 10% employer cost plus EC, never net the employer share against wages. **By the 10th**: remit with correct IDs; file the quarterly collection list at quarter-end. **January**: reconcile payroll registers to the Annual Register and file it. **Permits**: secure SSS clearance for the LGU license. **Delinquency**: accrue 2%/month, expect tax-like collection within 20 years — and never fund operations from withheld contributions past 30 days, the estafa line.

**Trap**: the 3%-per-month penalty in pre-2019 cases is history — RA 11199 imposes **2%**. **Trap**: Sec. 28(e) is OR generally but AND for register/deduct/remit — read the proviso. **Trap**: an SSS number at hiring never excuses the Sec. 24(a) report. **Trap**: employee benefits survive employer non-remittance — the worker still claims; the employer still pays (Secs. 22(b), 24).

**Exam memory set**: 15% (10/5), MSC P5,000–P35,000, Cirs. 2024-006–010, 1 Jan 2025; remit by the 10th, 2%/month, 20 years; report immediately, 30-day damage grace, January register, 5-day clearance; MPF above P20,000; EC P10/P30; Sec. 28 and/or map + 30-day estafa presumption.

Self-check: (1) An employer withholds January contributions but remits them on March 5 — what penalties and presumptions apply? (2) A contractor's worker is injured; the contractor never remitted — who else answers, and on what security? (3) A creditor seeks to garnish a retiree's SSS pension for a bank loan — what is the result?

Takeaways: SSS money runs on one schedule (today 15%, 10/5, MSC P5,000–P35,000, eff. 1 Jan 2025) applied to every member class; employers withhold, add their unshiftable share, and remit by the 10th under quarterly lists and January registers; benefits are tax- and garnishment-proof except for SSS debts; and failure compounds fast — 2% monthly, lost-benefit damages, tax-like collection within 20 years, and criminal liability up to presumed estafa, with corporate civil liability surviving any officer's acquittal.
